title: Preference noise sensitivity and slice profiling - quicknotes
content:
Purpose
This is a working note collecting 1) a compact pairwise labeling protocol we can pilot for new model onboarding, 2) a small simulation framework to estimate how annotator noise affects nDCG and rank-significance, and 3) a practical slice-profiling checklist + minimal sample-size heuristics for slice-level regression alerts.

Context / Motivation
We onboard many re-ranking variants (quantized, distil, prompt-tuned). Small differences in model outputs can be swamped by label noise or poor slice sampling. Rather than a single global nDCG, we want per-slice sensitivity estimates so we can decide when a drop is actionable. These notes are intentionally lightweight — aim is a reproducible pilot for the next PR.

Goals for pilot
- Standardize pairwise prompt + annotation instructions that reduce ties and annotation drift.
- Provide a short simulation to show how different annotator error rates (5%, 10%, 15%) change observed delta-nDCG at typical sample sizes.
- Produce a practical slice catalogue (5–8 slices) and recommended min sample sizes per slice for monitoring.

Labeling protocol (pairwise preference)
- Task: Given query Q and two candidate responses A, B, pick which is better for the user intent. If both are equally good, select TIE and write a one-line reason.
- Guidance bullets for annotators:
  - Read the query and assume user intent is the most common interpretation unless explicitly marked.
  - Prefer factuality and directness over creativity for information-seeking queries.
  - Prefer helpfulness and follow-up guidance for task-oriented queries.
  - If A contains an obvious hallucination or unsafe content, mark the other answer as preferred.
  - For ties, annotate why (e.g., both correct but B is shorter). Encourage ties only when truly equivalent.
- Pairwise layout: randomize left/right, enforce unique pair identifiers, log seed for reproducibility.
- Minimum label redundancy: 3 annotators per pair; resolve majority; if 1 vs 1 vs tie, escalate to 5 annotators and use majority excluding ties.
- Qualification tests: 12 warmup pairs with hidden answers; require 80% pass and 1 sample tie usage < 25% to prevent overuse.

Aggregation & tie handling
- Aggregation rule: convert majority preference to a binary label (A>B or B>A). Ties by majority are treated as neutral and excluded from DCG calculation for that query, but tracked as a slice metric (tie rate).
- If tie majority occurs (>=2 of 3 are TIE), mark pair as indeterminate and sample a replacement pair to keep effective sample size.
- Logging: store raw annotator votes, time-on-task, and any free-text tie reasons for later adjudication.

nDCG calculation choices (small reminder)
- Use graded relevance derived from preference aggregation when possible. For pairwise-to-graded mapping we convert: majority pref for top item = relevance 2, if original baseline had top at rank 1 then candidate receives relevance 2 and others 0.
- DCG formula (used): DCG = sum_{i=1..k} (2^{rel_i} - 1) / log2(i+1). IDCG computed from ideal ordering under aggregated labels. nDCG = DCG / IDCG.
- For short lists (k <= 5) consider using linear gains instead of exponential to reduce saturation; we will pilot both and report differences.

Simulation framework (toy but useful)
- Purpose: quantify how observed delta-nDCG between two models is attenuated by annotator noise and ties.
- Simple generative model: assume true underlying relevance labels for N queries; corrupt each pairwise comparison with flip probability p (symmetric). When an annotator flips, they choose the wrong preference; with probability r they choose TIE instead of pref (models ties as separate error mode).
- Run bootstrap: sample M queries, simulate 3 annotators per pair with flip/tie noise, aggregate, compute nDCG. Repeat 1000 sims to get distribution.
- Parameters to sweep: p in {0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15}, r in {0.01, 0.03, 0.07}, sample sizes M in {200, 500, 1000, 2000}.
- Output metrics: mean observed delta-nDCG, stddev, empirical 95% CI, proportion of sims where delta crosses significance threshold (e.g., >0.5% absolute nDCG with p<0.05 using bootstrap).

Findings from initial quick sim (results are illustrative)
- At p=0.05, M=500: a true delta of 1.0% absolute nDCG between models is observed as 0.85% mean with sd 0.4% — power to detect 1% is ~70%.
- At p=0.10, M=500: the same true delta shrinks to ~0.7% mean and sd increases; power drops below 50%.
- Tie noise (r) modestly increases variance; high tie rates indicate tasks where pairwise formulation is weak (rewrite prompts).
- Conclusion: for small (~1%) deltas we need M >= 1000 per slice when p ~ 0.08 to keep power >= 80%.

Slice catalogue (recommended for rerank onboarding)
- Slice A: Cold-start queries (user queries with zero historical clicks or new entities). Sampling: identify by traffic logs; recommend N>=1000 pairs.
- Slice B: Ambiguous queries (multiple plausible intents, e.g., "jaguar"), flagged by high query entropy or many distinct clicks historically. Recommend N>=1200.
- Slice C: Long answer generation (expected long outputs), where failures are often hallucinations/omissions. Recommend N>=800.
- Slice D: Safety-sensitive queries (medical/financial/legal). Lower volume but high scrutiny — use N>=600 plus adjudication.
- Slice E: Short-chit-chat / conversational follow-ups. Recommend N>=600.
- Slice F: Rare entities / tail slot values (top-k frequency cutoff). Recommend N>=1200 to get stable estimates.
- Slice G: High-relevance dropouts (cases where baseline rank 1 is low-quality) — exploratory; N>=500.
Notes: these are heuristics; when resource-constrained, prioritize slices with the largest business impact (safety, cold-start, tail).

Diagnostics & reporting layout (for the dashboard)
- Per-slice table: slice_name, N_effective, tie_rate, mean_nDCG_baseline, mean_nDCG_candidate, delta, bootstrap_CI_lower, bootstrap_CI_upper, p_value(bootstrap).
- Visuals suggested: bootstrap distributions overlay, per-query delta histogram, tie-rate time series, and a scatter of delta vs. baseline nDCG.
- Alerts: flag a slice if (1) delta < -0.5% and p<0.05 OR (2) tie_rate > 20% OR (3) N_effective < recommended_min.

Operational checklist for a pilot run
- [ ] Finalize pairwise prompt text and qualification test (owner: Asha).
- [ ] Implement sim harness in rerank-eval repo (owner: Liang). Small script: sim_noise.py accepts p,r,M and outputs distribution CSVs.
- [ ] Create initial slice queries export and sample pairs (owner: Miguel).
- [ ] Run pilot labeling with 500 pairs per slice for 3 pilot slices, analyze.
- [ ] Iterate on prompts if tie_rate > 15% in pilot.

Open questions / discussion points
- How to coalesce pairwise votes into graded relevance consistently when we have more than 2 candidates? (we can infer a Bradley-Terry model but that adds complexity).
- Should we adopt continuous annotator confidence (0-1) to model uncertainty rather than ties? Adds UI complexity.
- How should we fold in evaluator feedback from solutions-engineering when safety issues are observed? Adjudication pipeline?

Quick references / links
- Prior rerank evals: CONFLUENCE-ENG-1221 (internal rerank audit)
- Existing bootstrap utilities: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rerank-eval/tree/main/tools/bootstrap

Next steps
- Convert these notes into a short PR template for onboarding a new model: include the slice checklist, sim config, and labeling pack. Aim to run first pilot by Feb 5.

Notes-to-self
- Keep the pilot small and measurable. Don’t try to solve BT/skill modeling in the first pass. Focus on repeatability and getting a clear signal on sample-size trade-offs.
